text:
B: Oh, hello. Can you hear me?
A: Yeah. Graham.
B: Hi, Graham, I'm Joanne. Erm, I'm in Basingstoke.
A: Tipton.
B: Is that the West Midlands?
A: Black Country.
B: Right. Sorry, I'm not very good at geography north of Oxford, which is awful because I did it at university.
A: It's alright.
B: Erm. Is this your last call as well?
A: Ar. Fourth.
B: I'm quite tired, to be honest. Knackered, actually. I'm not very good at talking to new people.
A: Me neither. Sandra signed me up. The wife.
B: Oh, gosh. Did she ask you first?
A: After.
B: Ha. My partner Mark would do something like that. Erm, what did you used to do, Graham? Or are you still working?
A: Retired. Toolmaker, I was. Then maintenance fitter.
B: Oh, so you'd be reading drawings, then?
A: All day. Engineering drawings. Tolerances, that sort of thing.
B: I do that, sort of. Not engineering, building plans. I'm a planner at the council, so people's extensions mostly. I'm always squinting at elevations.
A: Council. Yow lot keep messing our bins about.
B: Oh no, that's not us, I promise. That's a different department. Different council, even. But I'm sorry, it's always the bins people are cross about.
A: Every other week now. Then they change the day.
B: That's very annoying. My dad used to say the same. He worked for the Post Office, and he'd always notice if the bin men were late.
A: Ar. You notice. When you've been on shifts.
B: What was the best bit of your job, do you think?
A: Er... making something right. First time. You'd set the lathe up, take a cut, measure it. Spot on. That were a good feeling. Did me apprenticeship at a firm that's gone now. Whole street's gone.
B: That's sad. I'm sorry.
A: It's how it is.
B: Do you still make things, at home?
A: Shed. Got a mower engine in bits. Not finished it.
B: Mark's the same. He's had a shelf half-built in the hallway since spring. I'm not sure that's very helpful, sorry.
A: No. It's alright.
B: I think we're about out of time. It was nice talking to you, Graham.
A: Yow too. Tara.
